newsitem.title: ESTONIA: ANALYSIS-ESTONIA SHARES BOOM, WILL GAINS SPREAD?.
newsitem.headline: ANALYSIS-ESTONIA SHARES BOOM, WILL GAINS SPREAD?.

text.p: Estonian shares have kept hitting new records this week and dealers and commentators said they saw no end in sight yet to the boom in volumes and prices.
They also said that the market enthusiasm may spill over into Latvia and Lithuania in what would be a repeat performance of January's pan-Baltic stock boom.
"There is still no big selling pressure," said Gunnar Maemets, securities specialist at Forekspank.
The boom in Tallinn started with good interest from foreign investors in Hansapank and Uhispank, both of which are listed on the Helsinki stock exchange.
"It started with foreign investors. They were buying Hansapank stocks and this took the market up," said Charlie Viikberg, trader at Houipank.
Foreign interest may have started the boom, but small local investors are fuelling it.
The volume on the Estonian market reached 115 million kroons in trade on Thursday almost double volumes earlier in the week.
"Bascially the boom is fuelled by local buying pressure, the increase in volume was helped by foreign investors selling stocks off," said Katrin Kaarli, senior Hansapank analyst.
And the interest is still there, with strong demand for shares, especially for Hansapank.

"Investors are mostly looking for banks shares and they hope that the companies will revise and raise their profit estimates for 1997 especially for Hansapank and Hoiupank," said Sander Danil, equities analyst with Tallinna Pank.
"Expectations for first quarter results are high," he added.
Dealers and analysts also said the market boom could spread to neighbouring Latvia and Lithuania.
"It is normal that this sort of rise in Tallinn will impact on the Latvian and Lithuanian markets," said Riho Talumae, trader from Talinvest, a pan-Baltic investment bank.
"It is possible that some investors will get out of Estonia and move to Russia and Lithuania, where there are good price opportunities," said Tallinna Pank's Danil.
Hansapank, which has a subsidiary in Latvia and will open a brokerage in Lithuania, also believes it will spread.
"Such a rise is infectious. Our brokers market the three countries as a group, so it is likely to spread," said Kaarli.
But it is not just the Estonians who are expecting the rise, Lithuanians are also watching what happens in Tallinn.

"Things are slow now, but the market should become active soon...The Estonian market seems to have hit its peak, and there are signals that investors from there will soon switch to Lithuania," one Vilnius dealer told Reuters.
